query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A reduced cooling rate during the solution heat treatment of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of serrated grain boundaries via coarsening of precipitates, which in turn improves elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the alloy processed with conventional rapid cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti-Ni-(Cr,Co,Fe)) fabricated to meet the high-entropy criteria with components between 5–35 at% each, possessing a conventional as-processed microstructure with predominantly straight grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled, reduced cooling rate during the solution heat treatment so that coarsening of precipitates (e.g., a γ′ phase) occurs sufficiently to interact with grain boundaries and drive them to develop a serrated morphology.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature applications around 650°C, with heat treatment durations adjusted (e.g., 1–100 h) to allow precipitate coarsening. The alloy must adhere to high-entropy specifications with titanium and nickel as the primary components, and the processing window is limited to cooling rates that enable precipitate coarsening but prevent overgrowth or degradation of the microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated grain boundaries formed due to precipitate-induced undulations along the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Serrated grain boundaries help distribute local strains more evenly and reduce stress concentration along the boundaries, thereby mitigating intergranular cracking and hot ductility drops at elevated temperatures during tensile and creep loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy processed with the reduced cooling rate is expected to exhibit significantly improved high-temperature mechanical properties, evidenced by increased tensile fracture strain and enhanced creep rupture life compared to the same alloy processed with conventional rapid cooling.
generation.baseline: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy processed with standard rapid cooling heat treatment, yielding straight grain boundaries and showing typical high-temperature ductility drops.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective within a thermal operating range near 600–700°C and for controlled annealing times that permit optimal precipitate coarsening. Deviations outside these boundaries may result in either insufficient grain boundary modification or deleterious overgrowth of microstructural features.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of improvement (e.g., the exact factors of increase in tensile strain or creep life) remains uncertain and will depend on the precise cooling rate, alloy composition nuances, and heat treatment duration. There is also inherent uncertainty regarding the kinetics of precipitate coarsening in this novel alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy samples that are identical in composition and initial processing. Process one set via conventional rapid cooling after solution heat treatment (control) and the other set with a controlled, reduced cooling rate expected to promote precipitate coarsening and serrated grain boundary formation. Characterize microstructural features using scanning electron microscopy and test both sets using tensile and creep experiments at 650°C.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology (e.g., degree of serration via SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the reduced cooling rate treatment does not yield a statistically significant (e.g., ≥10%) increase in tensile fracture strain or creep rupture life relative to the control, and/or if microstructural characterization fails to reveal the formation of serrated grain boundaries in the treated samples.

## Abstract
ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
